key_takeaway: You must notify the unsuccessful bidders within three days after the award is made. It's a mandatory courtesy.

content: If a contractor discovers a mistake after award, it must be processed under the procedures of Part 33 (Disputes). Correction is only possible if it's based on clear and convincing evidence and doesn't change the essential requirements of the contract.
key_takeaway: Fixing a mistake after an award is much harder and is handled as a formal dispute. You need 'clear and convincing evidence' to even consider reforming or rescinding the contract.

topic: Reforming a Contract for a Mistake
content: An agency can reform a contract to increase the price only if the corrected price does not exceed that of the next lowest acceptable bid under the original invitation.
key_takeaway: If you agree to correct a mistake by increasing the contract price, the new price can't be higher than what the second-place bidder offered.

topic: Rescinding a Contract for a Mistake
content: Agencies are authorized to make a determination to rescind a contract due to a mistake in bid, based on clear and convincing evidence that a mistake was made.
key_takeaway: A contract can be completely canceled (rescinded) because of a mistake, but only if the evidence for the mistake is rock solid.

content: A mistake can be corrected after award only if it was mutual OR if it was a unilateral mistake by the contractor that was so apparent as to have charged the contracting officer with notice of the probability of the mistake.
key_takeaway: To fix a contractor's mistake after award, the error must have been so obvious that the CO should have reasonably noticed it (e.g., a bid that is 10x lower than all others).

content: For policies and procedures related to cost and price negotiation for contract modifications, see FAR Part 15.
key_takeaway: When you need to price a modification to a sealed bid contract, the rules you follow are found in FAR Part 15, not Part 14.

content: When an IFB does not contain an economic price adjustment (EPA) clause but a bidder proposes one with a ceiling, the bid must be evaluated based on the maximum possible price with the adjustment.
key_takeaway: If a bidder adds their own Economic Price Adjustment clause with a ceiling, you must evaluate their bid at its worst-case (highest) price.

content: Noncompetitive, or sole source, acquisition is a process whereby an award is made to a single vendor without soliciting offers from multiple sources. When using this acquisition strategy, agencies should remove unnecessary information and requirements from the request for proposal (RFP), including voluminous proposal preparation instructions and evaluation factors.
key_takeaway: When going sole source, RFPs should be streamlined to remove unnecessary requirements since there's only one vendor to consider.

content: Exchanges of information among all interested parties are encouraged and can occur at any time between the identification of a requirement through the receipt of proposals. These exchanges can improve both the Government's understanding of industry capabilities and the industry's understanding of the Government's needs.
key_takeaway: Communicating with industry early and often is encouraged to ensure everyone is on the same page about the requirement and what industry can offer.

content: Agencies are encouraged to release requests for information (RFI) when the Government does not currently intend to award a contract, but wants to obtain price, delivery, market, or capabilities information for planning purposes. Responses to RFIs are not offers and cannot be accepted by the Government to form a binding contract.
key_takeaway: RFIs are for market research, not for awarding contracts. Industry's responses are just information, not official offers.

content: Agencies may publish a notice that provides a general description of the scope or purpose of the acquisition and invites potential offerors to submit information that allows the Government to advise offerors about their potential to be viable competitors. Informing respondents that they are 'not viable' does not prevent them from participating in the resultant acquisition.
key_takeaway: The government can use an advisory multistep process to give vendors a heads-up on their competitive viability, but even 'non-viable' vendors can still compete.

topic: Structuring RFPs: Uniform Contract Format Exceptions
content: Agencies do not need to use the uniform contract format for: (i) Construction and architect-engineer contracts, (ii) Subsistence contracts, (iii) Supplies or services contracts requiring special contract formats... (iv) Streamlined RFPs, (v) Contracts exempted by the agency head or designee.
key_takeaway: The standard Uniform Contract Format isn't required for certain acquisitions like construction, A-E services, or when using a streamlined RFP.

content: The tradeoff approach to source selection is appropriate when it may be in the Government's best interest to consider award to other than the lowest priced offeror or other than the highest technically rated offeror. This process permits tradeoffs among cost or price and non-cost or non-price factors.
key_takeaway: The tradeoff process allows the government to award to a higher-priced offer if its technical or other benefits are worth the extra cost.

content: The LPTA source selection approach must only be used when the agency can comprehensively and clearly describe the minimum requirements and would realize no, or minimal, value from a proposal that exceeds the minimum technical or performance requirements.
key_takeaway: Only use LPTA when requirements are crystal clear and there is no benefit to paying more for a 'better' proposal.

content: Phased acquisitions break down complex or high-risk acquisitions into distinct parts for contract award. Instead of a single and comprehensive proposal and evaluation process, phased acquisitions are structured to make separate awards at distinct phases of the acquisition.
key_takeaway: For complex, high-risk programs, a phased acquisition allows the government to award contracts for individual stages, reducing risk and increasing flexibility.

content: Price or cost to the Government must be evaluated in every competitive source selection. Proposed price reductions under an offeror's other contracts cannot be used as an evaluation factor.
key_takeaway: Price or cost must always be evaluated in a competitive acquisition. Discounts on other contracts don't count toward the current evaluation.

content: Past performance must be evaluated in every competitive source selection, unless the contracting officer documents the reason past performance is not an appropriate evaluation factor for the acquisition.
key_takeaway: Past performance must be an evaluation factor unless the contracting officer provides a written justification for leaving it out.

content: The RFP must...state, at a minimum, whether all evaluation factors other than cost or price, when combined, are—(1) Significantly more important than cost or price; (2) Approximately equal to cost or price; or (3) Significantly less important than cost or price.
key_takeaway: The RFP must clearly state the relative importance of non-cost/price factors compared to the cost/price itself.

content: Oral presentations may be used as a substitute for requesting portions of a written proposal information from offerors. Information on an offeror's capability, past performance, work plans or approaches, staffing resources, transition plans, or sample tasks can be suitable for oral presentations.
key_takeaway: Oral presentations can replace parts of a written proposal and are useful for evaluating things like capability, work plans, and past performance.

content: When the Government changes its requirements or terms and conditions, the contracting officer must amend the RFP. Amendments issued before the established time and date for receipt of proposals must be issued to all parties receiving the RFP.
key_takeaway: If the government's needs change before proposals are due, the contracting officer must issue an official amendment to all potential offerors.

content: Any proposal, modification, or revision, that is received at the designated Government office after the exact time specified for receipt of proposals is 'late' and will not be considered, unless it is received before award is made, the contracting officer determines that accepting the late proposal would not unduly delay the acquisition...
key_takeaway: A late proposal is automatically rejected unless it arrives before award, won't cause a delay, and meets one of the strict exceptions.

content: A late modification of an otherwise successful proposal, that makes its terms more favorable to the Government, will be considered at any time it is received and may be accepted by the contracting officer.
key_takeaway: Even after the deadline, a late modification from the winning offeror can be accepted if it makes the deal better for the government.

content: If any portion of a proposal submitted electronically is unreadable, contracting officers must immediately notify the offeror and permit the offeror to resubmit the unreadable portion of the proposal. ...the resubmission is considered as if it were received at the date and time of the original unreadable submission.
key_takeaway: If a proposal is electronically corrupted or unreadable, the offeror gets a chance to resubmit it, and it will be treated as if it arrived on time.

content: Clarifications are exchanges between the Government and offerors where offerors are given the opportunity to resolve minor or clerical errors or clarify certain aspects of their proposal. Clarifications do not permit offerors to revise their proposal and cannot be used to cure proposal deficiencies or material omissions.
key_takeaway: Clarifications are for clearing up minor errors or ambiguities; they are not an opportunity for an offeror to fix a deficient or incomplete proposal.

content: Contracting officers may make competitive awards without negotiations if the RFP states that the Government intends to evaluate proposals and make award without negotiation. If the RFP includes such a notice and the Government determines it is necessary to negotiate, the rationale for doing so must be documented in the contract file.
key_takeaway: The government can award without discussions if the RFP says so, but if they change their mind and decide to negotiate, they must document why.

content: A competitive range is the group of evaluated proposals that the contracting officer determines are best suited for further negotiation. Contracting officers must establish a competitive range if negotiations will occur after evaluating competitive proposals.
key_takeaway: The competitive range consists of the top-tier proposals that the government considers to be the most likely candidates for award.

content: The source selection decision must represent the SSA's independent judgement and be based on a comparative assessment of proposals against all source selection criteria in the RFP. The source selection decision must be documented and include the rationale for any business judgments and tradeoffs made or relied on by the SSA.
key_takeaway: The Source Selection Authority (SSA) makes the final award decision based on a comparative assessment of proposals against the RFP's criteria, and this decision must be well-documented.

content: Contracting officers must notify offerors promptly in writing when their proposals are excluded from the competitive range or otherwise eliminated from the competition. The notice must state the basis for the determination and that proposal revisions will not be considered.
key_takeaway: If a proposal is kicked out of the competition, the contracting officer must send a written notice explaining why, and making it clear that the proposal cannot be revised.

content: Offerors may request a preaward debriefing by submitting a written request for debriefing to the contracting officer within 3 days after receipt of the notice of exclusion from the competition. If the offeror does not submit a timely request, the offeror need not be given either a preaward or a postaward debriefing.
key_takeaway: An offeror has 3 days from receiving notice of exclusion to request a preaward debriefing in writing. Miss that window, and you may not get a debriefing at all.

content: At a minimum, preaward debriefings must include—(i) The agency's evaluation of significant elements in the offeror's proposal; (ii) A summary of the rationale for eliminating the offeror from the competition; and (iii) Reasonable responses to relevant questions about whether source selection procedures were followed.
key_takeaway: A preaward debriefing must cover the evaluation of significant elements, the reason for elimination, and answers to questions about the process.

content: Preaward debriefings must not disclose— (1) The number of offerors; (2) The identity of other offerors; (3) The content of other offerors proposals; (4) The ranking of other offerors; (5) The evaluation of other offerors...
key_takeaway: In a preaward debriefing, you can't be told who else is competing, what's in their proposals, or how they were ranked or evaluated.

content: Within 3 days after the date of contract award, contracting officers must provide written notification to each offeror whose proposal was in the competitive range but was not selected for award... The notice must include the number of offerors solicited, the number of proposals received, and the name and address of each offeror receiving an award.
key_takeaway: Within 3 days of award, all unsuccessful offerors in the competitive range must be notified in writing about who won and how many companies competed.

content: Offerors may request a postaward debriefing by submitting a written request for the debriefing to the contracting officer within 3 days after receipt of the award notice... To the maximum extent practicable, the debriefing should occur within 5 days after receipt of the written request.
key_takeaway: An offeror has 3 days from receiving the award notice to request a postaward debriefing, which should ideally happen within 5 days of the request.

content: At a minimum, the debriefing information must include...the Government's evaluation of the significant weaknesses or deficiencies in the offeror's proposal; the overall evaluated cost or price and technical rating of the successful offeror and the debriefed offeror; and a summary of the rationale for award.
key_takeaway: A postaward debriefing reveals your proposal's weaknesses/deficiencies, a side-by-side comparison of your rating and the winner's, and the justification for the award decision.

content: The debriefing must not include point-by-point comparisons of the debriefed offeror's proposal with those of other offerors. Moreover, the debriefing must not reveal...trade secrets; privileged or confidential manufacturing processes and techniques; [or] commercial and financial information that is privileged or confidential...
key_takeaway: Even in a postaward debriefing, the government cannot do a point-by-point comparison with other proposals or reveal other companies' trade secrets and confidential financial data.

content: Mistakes in a contractor's proposal that are disclosed after award must be processed substantially in accordance with the procedures for mistakes in bids in part 14.
key_takeaway: If a mistake is found in a contractor's proposal after the contract has already been awarded, the process for handling it follows the rules for 'mistakes in bids' from FAR Part 14.

content: In establishing the reasonableness of the offered prices, contracting officers must—(1) Obtain certified cost or pricing data when required...; or (2) When certified cost or pricing data are not required..., obtain data other than certified cost or pricing data as necessary to establish a fair and reasonable price.
key_takeaway: To determine a fair price, the contracting officer must get either certified cost or pricing data or, if that's not required, other data to support the price.

topic: Data Other Than Certified Cost or Pricing Data: Order of Preference
content: For acquisitions that do not require certified cost or pricing data, contracting officers must generally use the following order of preference...: (1) No additional data from the offeror, when adequate price competition exists... (2) Data related to prices... (3) Cost data...
key_takeaway: When certified data isn't needed, the preferred data is: first, nothing (if competition is adequate); second, price data; and last, cost data.

topic: Prohibition on Obtaining Certified Cost or Pricing Data
content: Contracting officers must not require certified cost or pricing data to support any contracts, subcontracts, or modifications—(1) When...prices agreed upon are based on adequate price competition; (2) When...prices agreed upon are based on prices set by law or regulation; (3) When a commercial product or commercial service is being acquired...
key_takeaway: Certified cost or pricing data cannot be required when the price is based on adequate competition, set by law, or for a commercial product/service.

content: A price is based on adequate price competition when—(A) Two or more responsible offerors, competing independently, submit priced offers that satisfy the Government's expressed requirement; [and] (B) Award will be made to the offeror whose proposal represents the best value where price is a substantial factor...
key_takeaway: The gold standard for 'adequate price competition' is receiving two or more independent, responsible offers for a best value award where price is a substantial factor.

topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data Threshold
content: Unless an exception...applies, contracting officers must obtain certified cost or pricing data when an action meets or exceeds the threshold of $2.5 million (for prime contracts awarded on or after July 1, 2018).
key_takeaway: Certified cost or pricing data is required for contract actions of $2.5 million or more (post-July 2018) unless a specific exception applies.

content: The objective of proposal analysis is to ensure that the final agreed-to price is fair and reasonable. Contracting officers are responsible for evaluating the reasonableness of the offered prices. The complexity and circumstances of each acquisition should determine the level of detail of the analysis required.
key_takeaway: The whole point of analyzing a proposal is to ensure the final price is fair and reasonable, and the level of effort for this analysis should match the complexity of the buy.

content: The Government may use various price analysis techniques...including, but not limited to, the following: (1) Comparison of proposed prices received in response to the RFP. (2) Comparison of the proposed prices to historical prices paid...
key_takeaway: The two preferred price analysis techniques are comparing offers received against each other and comparing them to historical prices paid for the same or similar items.

content: Cost analysis is the review and evaluation of any separate cost elements and profit or fee in an offeror's or contractor's proposal, as needed to determine a fair and reasonable price or to determine cost realism. Cost analysis must be used when certified cost or pricing data are required.
key_takeaway: Cost analysis involves breaking down and evaluating the individual cost elements (like labor, materials, profit) and must be used whenever certified cost or pricing data is required.

content: Cost realism analyses must be performed on cost-reimbursement contacts to determine the probable cost of performance for each offeror. The probable cost may differ from the proposed cost and should reflect the Government's best estimate of the cost of any contract that is most likely to result from the offeror's proposal.
key_takeaway: For cost-reimbursement contracts, the government must perform a cost realism analysis to determine its own 'probable cost' estimate, which may be different from what the offeror proposed.

content: Unbalanced pricing exists when, despite an acceptable total evaluated price, the price of one or more line items is significantly over or understated as indicated by the application of cost or price analysis techniques. An offer may be rejected if the contracting officer determines that the lack of balance poses an unacceptable risk to the Government.
key_takeaway: Unbalanced pricing, where some line items are priced too high and others too low, can be rejected if the contracting officer believes it poses an unacceptable risk.

content: Contracting officers are responsible for the determination of a fair and reasonable price for the prime contract, including subcontracting costs. To support this effort, the prime contractor or subcontractor must—(1) Conduct appropriate cost or price analyses to establish the reasonableness of proposed subcontract prices...
key_takeaway: Prime contractors are required to conduct their own cost/price analysis on their subcontractors to justify that those sub-prices are reasonable.

content: Agencies making noncompetitive contract awards over $100,000 totaling $50 million or more a year—(i) Must use a structured approach for determining the profit or fee objective in those acquisitions that require cost analysis...; and (ii) May prescribe specific exemptions for situations in which mandatory use of a structured approach would be clearly inappropriate.
key_takeaway: Large agencies must use a structured approach (like a weighted guidelines method) to determine profit objectives for noncompetitive awards that require cost analysis.

content: Must not negotiate a price or fee that exceeds the following statutory limitations... (i) For experimental, developmental, or research work performed under a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract, the fee must not exceed 15 percent of the contract's estimated cost, excluding fee. ... (iii) For other cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts, the fee must not exceed 10 percent of the contract's estimated cost, excluding fee.
key_takeaway: There are statutory caps on profit: for CPFF contracts, the fee cannot exceed 15% for R&D work or 10% for all other work.

content: This factor measures the complexity of the work and the resources required of the prospective contractor for contract performance. Greater profit opportunity should be provided under contracts requiring a high degree of professional and managerial skill and to prospective contractors whose skills, facilities, and technical assets can be expected to lead to efficient and economical contract performance.
key_takeaway: A key factor in setting profit is 'Contractor Effort'—more complex work requiring greater skill, resources, and efficiency from the contractor should be rewarded with a higher profit opportunity.

topic: Profit Analysis Factors: Contract Cost Risk
content: This factor measures the degree of cost responsibility and associated risk that the prospective contractor will assume as a result of the contract type... The contractor assumes the greatest cost risk in a closely priced firm-fixed-price contract... [and] the least cost risk in a cost-plus-fixed-fee level-of-effort contract.
key_takeaway: Profit should reflect the level of cost risk the contractor takes on. A firm-fixed-price (FFP) contract carries the highest risk and thus warrants higher profit, while a cost-plus-fixed-fee (CPFF) carries the lowest.

content: Contracting officers may require offerors to submit make-or-buy program plans for acquisitions requiring certified cost or pricing data whose estimated value is $20 million or more... Contracting officers may only require offerors to submit make-or-buy programs for acquisitions whose estimated value is under $20 million if the contracting officer determines that the information is necessary and documents the reasons...
key_takeaway: A make-or-buy plan may be required for acquisitions over $20M that need certified data. For acquisitions under $20M, it can only be required if the CO justifies the specific need in writing.

content: The information required from an offeror about a make-or-buy program must— (i) Be confined to those major items or work efforts that normally would require company management review... (ii) Not include raw materials, products, commercial services, and off-the-shelf items, unless their potential impact on contract cost or schedule is critical...
key_takeaway: A make-or-buy plan should focus only on major, complex items needing management review, not routine materials or commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) items unless they are critical to cost or schedule.

content: Contracting officers will use FPRA rates as bases for pricing all contracts, modifications, and other contractual actions to be performed during the period covered by the agreement. Conditions that may affect the agreement's validity must be reported promptly to the administrative contracting officer (ACO).
key_takeaway: An FPRA provides pre-approved rates (like overhead and G&A) to be used for all pricing actions during a specific period, but anything that might invalidate the agreement must be reported to the ACO immediately.

content: Should-cost reviews are a specialized form of cost analysis. Should-cost reviews differ from traditional evaluation methods because they do not assume that a contractor's historical costs reflect efficient and economical operation. Instead, these reviews evaluate the economy and efficiency of the contractor's existing work force, methods, materials, equipment, real property, operating systems, and management.
key_takeaway: A 'should-cost' review doesn't accept a contractor's past costs as efficient. It's a deep dive to determine what a product or service *should* cost if the contractor were operating economically.

topic: When to Consider a Program Should-Cost Review
content: A program should-cost review should be considered, particularly in the case of a major system acquisition, when—(i) Some initial production has already taken place; (ii) The contract will be awarded on a sole source basis; [and] (iii) There are future year production requirements for substantial quantities of like items...
key_takeaway: A should-cost review is best suited for a major sole-source program that has already started initial production and has large future orders.

content: The purpose of performing cost or price analysis is to develop a negotiation position that permits the contracting officer and the offeror an opportunity to reach agreement on a fair and reasonable price. A fair and reasonable price does not require that agreement be reached on every element of cost...
key_takeaway: The goal of negotiation is to agree on a total price that is fair and reasonable, not to win an argument on every single cost element.

content: The contracting officer's primary concern is the overall price the Government will actually pay. The contracting officer's objective is to negotiate a contract of a type and with a price providing the contractor the greatest incentive for efficient and economical performance.
key_takeaway: The CO's main goal in negotiation is to get the best overall price for the government while incentivizing the contractor to perform efficiently.

content: Contracting officers must document in the contract file the principal elements of the negotiated agreement. The documentation (e.g., price negotiation memorandum) must include... (1) The purpose of the negotiation. (2) A description of the acquisition... (3) The name, position, and organization of each person representing the contractor and the Government...
key_takeaway: A Price Negotiation Memorandum (PNM) must document the basics of the negotiation, including its purpose, a description of the acquisition, and who was at the table.

content: Unsolicited proposals allow unique and innovative ideas or approaches developed outside the Government to be made available to Government agencies for use in accomplishing their missions.
key_takeaway: An unsolicited proposal is a way for a company to pitch a unique and innovative idea to the government on its own initiative.

content: Government personnel should not use any data, concept, idea, or other part of an unsolicited proposal as the basis, or part of the basis, for a RFP or in negotiations with any other firm unless the offeror is notified of and agrees to the intended use.
key_takeaway: The government cannot take an idea from a company's unsolicited proposal and use it in a competitive RFP without that company's permission.

content: A valid unsolicited proposal must— (1) Be innovative and unique; (2) Be independently originated and developed by the offeror; (3) Be prepared without Government supervision, endorsement, direction, or direct Government involvement...
key_takeaway: To be considered valid, an unsolicited proposal must be an innovative and unique idea developed independently by the offeror, without any government involvement.

content: Advertising material, commercial product or commercial service offers, contributions, or routine correspondence on technical issues, are not unsolicited proposals.
key_takeaway: Marketing brochures, standard commercial offers, or casual technical suggestions are not considered valid unsolicited proposals.

content: If the offeror wishes to restrict the use and disclosure of data, the title page must be marked [with a specific] legend... The offeror must also mark each sheet of data it wishes to restrict with the following legend: Use or disclosure of data contained on this sheet is subject to the restriction on the title page of this proposal.
key_takeaway: If you want to protect the data in an unsolicited proposal, you must apply the specific restrictive legend to both the title page and every individual sheet containing protected data.

content: When evaluating unsolicited proposals, evaluators should consider, at a minimum, the following factors: (1) Unique, innovative and meritorious methods...; (2) Overall scientific, technical, or socioeconomic merits...; (3) Potential contribution of the effort to the agency's specific mission...
key_takeaway: An unsolicited proposal is evaluated based on its uniqueness, its technical and scientific merit, and its potential contribution to the agency's mission.

topic: Unsolicited Proposals: Justification for Sole Source
content: A favorable evaluation of an unsolicited proposal does not, in itself, justify awarding a contract without providing for full and open competition.
key_takeaway: Even if an unsolicited proposal gets a fantastic evaluation, that alone is not enough to justify a sole-source contract award.

content: Contracting officers may begin negotiations on a sole source basis only when— (a) An unsolicited proposal receives a favorable comprehensive evaluation; (b) A justification and approval is obtained in accordance with part 6; (c) The agency technical office sponsoring the contract furnishes the necessary funds; and (d) The requirements for synopsizing a proposed contract action are met.
key_takeaway: To award a sole-source contract from an unsolicited proposal, you need four things: a favorable evaluation, a J&A, funding from the technical office, and a public synopsis of the action.
